units.title: Electric current and circuits
units.key_idea: Electric current is the flow of charge through a closed path called a circuit; it is measured in amperes.
units.body:
When you switch on a bulb, electric charges start flowing through the wires. This flow of charge is called electric current.

Current flows only when there is a complete, closed path called a circuit. A simple circuit has:
1. A source, like a cell or battery, which pushes the charges.
2. Wires that carry the current.
3. A device, like a bulb, that uses the electricity.
4. A switch to open or close the path.

When the switch is on, the circuit is closed and the bulb glows. When it is off, there is a gap, the circuit is open, and no current flows.

Current is measured in amperes (A) using an ammeter, which is connected in series (in line) with the circuit.

Think of water in a pipe from a tank on the roof. The tank's height pushes the water, the pipe carries it, and a tap controls it. In a circuit, the battery pushes, the wire carries, and the switch controls.

Safety: Never touch bare wires or switches with wet hands. Household electricity can kill.

Current is the flow of charges through a conductor.

units.title: Voltage, resistance and Ohm's law
units.key_idea: Ohm's law: V = I × R. Voltage pushes current; resistance opposes it.
units.body:
Voltage (potential difference) is the push that makes charges flow. It is measured in volts (V) using a voltmeter, connected across (in parallel with) a device. A torch cell gives about 1.5 V. Indian home supply is about 220–230 V.

Resistance is how much a material opposes the flow of current. It is measured in ohms (Ω). Copper wire has very low resistance, so it is used for wiring. The thin coil (filament) inside an old bulb has high resistance, so it gets hot and glows.

Ohm's law connects them:
V = I × R
where V is voltage, I is current and R is resistance (at a constant temperature).

Example: a 12 V battery is connected to a 4 Ω resistor. Current I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 A.

Resistance of a wire increases when:
1. The wire is longer.
2. The wire is thinner.
It also depends on the material.

So for heavy appliances like a motor pump, electricians use thicker wire, so it doesn't heat up dangerously.
questions: 12 V across a 4 Ω resistor gives a current of:
It measures the difference across two points.
Why is copper used for house wiring?
Low resistance lets current flow with little heating.
Why do heavy appliances need thicker wires?
Thicker wires have less resistance and heat less
Thin wires heat up with large current and can cause fires.
About how much is Indian household voltage?
Indian homes get roughly 230 V AC.

units.title: Power and electrical safety
units.key_idea: Power P = V × I (watts); electricity bills count energy in kWh (units); fuses and earthing keep us safe.
units.body:
Electric power tells how fast a device uses energy. It is measured in watts (W).
P = V × I
A 230 V fan drawing 0.3 A uses about 69 W.

Your electricity bill counts energy, not power. Energy = Power × Time. The unit on the bill is the kilowatt-hour (kWh), also called a "unit". A 100 W bulb on for 10 hours uses 100 × 10 = 1000 Wh = 1 kWh = 1 unit.

So, to save money: switch off lights when not needed and prefer LED bulbs. A 9 W LED gives about as much light as a 60 W old bulb.

Safety devices:
1. Fuse or MCB: if too much current flows (overload or short circuit), the fuse melts or the MCB trips and cuts the supply, preventing fire.
2. Earthing: the green wire connects metal bodies of appliances to the ground, so a leak of current goes to the earth instead of through your body.

Safety: Never overload one socket with many plugs. Switch off the main supply before any repair, and call a licensed electrician for wiring work.
questions: A 100 W bulb used for 10 hours uses:
The 'unit' on an electricity bill is:
Bills charge for energy in kWh.
What does a fuse or MCB do?
Cuts the supply when too much current flows
It protects wiring from overload and short circuits.
Sending leaking current into the ground
Leakage flows to earth instead of through a person.
Which saves more electricity for the same light?
LEDs use far less power for similar light.
Before repairing any electrical fitting, you must:
Always cut the supply first, and call an electrician if unsure.
Why is overloading one socket dangerous?
Too much current can heat wires and cause a fire

units.title: Reflection of light
units.key_idea: Light bounces off smooth shiny surfaces; the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
units.body:
We see objects because light from them reaches our eyes. Light travels in straight lines.

When light hits a smooth, shiny surface like a mirror or still water, it bounces back. This is reflection.

The laws of reflection:
1. The angle at which light hits the mirror (angle of incidence) is equal to the angle at which it bounces off (angle of reflection).
2. The incoming ray, the reflected ray and the normal (an imaginary line standing straight up from the mirror) all lie in the same flat plane.

You can see this when you shine a torch at a mirror at a slant: the light bounces off at the same slant on the other side.

A plane (flat) mirror forms an image that is:
• the same size as the object,
• as far behind the mirror as the object is in front,
• upright,
• laterally inverted: your right hand looks like the left hand in the mirror. This is why AMBULANCE is written in reverse on the front of ambulances, so drivers read it correctly in their mirrors.
questions: Light bouncing off a mirror is called:
Bouncing back from a surface is reflection.
According to the law of reflection:
Angle of incidence = angle of reflection
A line perpendicular to the mirror

To read correctly in a driver's mirror
Mirrors laterally invert, so the reversed word appears correct.

You stand 2 m in front of a mirror. Your image is:
The image is as far behind as the object is in front.
That is why shadows have sharp shapes.

units.title: Spherical mirrors
units.key_idea: Concave mirrors curve inward and can focus light; convex mirrors curve outward and show a wider view.
units.body:
Take a shiny steel spoon. Its inside curve is like a concave mirror, and its back is like a convex mirror. These are spherical mirrors, parts of a hollow sphere.

Concave mirror (curved inward):
• It brings parallel rays of light together at a point called the focus.
• Close up, it makes a bigger, upright image. That is why it is used as a shaving or make-up mirror.
• Uses: torch and vehicle headlights (a bulb at the focus sends out a strong straight beam), dentists' mirrors, and solar cookers that focus sunlight to cook food.

Convex mirror (curved outward):
• It spreads light out.
• It always forms a small, upright image.
• It shows a much wider area.
• Use: rear-view mirrors in vehicles, and mirrors at sharp turns on hill roads, so drivers can see traffic around the bend.

The distance from the mirror to the focus is the focal length. For spherical mirrors, focal length is half of the radius of curvature: f = R/2.
questions: Which mirror is used as a vehicle's rear-view mirror?
Convex mirrors show a wider view.
A solar cooker uses which mirror to focus sunlight?
Concave mirrors bring light to a focus.
The inside of a shiny spoon acts like a:
A convex mirror always forms an image that is:
Convex mirrors give diminished, upright images.
Torch headlights use a concave mirror because:
A bulb at the focus gives a strong straight beam
Light from the focus reflects into a parallel beam.
Focal length f and radius of curvature R are related by:
Focal length is half the radius of curvature.
Mirrors at sharp hill-road turns are usually:
They let drivers see a wide area around the bend.
A shaving mirror is concave because close up it gives:
Near a concave mirror, the image is enlarged and upright.

units.title: Refraction of light
units.key_idea: Light bends when it passes from one material into another because its speed changes.
units.body:
Put a pencil in a glass of water. It looks bent at the water's surface. A pond also looks shallower than it really is. Both happen because of refraction.

Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one transparent material to another, like from air into water or glass. It happens because light travels at different speeds in different materials. Light is fastest in air (and vacuum), slower in water, and slower still in glass.

Rules:
1. Going from air into water or glass (into a denser medium), light slows down and bends towards the normal.
2. Coming out from water into air, light speeds up and bends away from the normal.

The refractive index tells how much a material slows light. Water's is about 1.33 and glass's about 1.5. A higher number means more bending.

Safety tip from science: because refraction makes water look shallower, never jump into a pond or canal assuming it is shallow.

Lenses in spectacles and cameras use refraction to focus light. A convex lens (thicker in the middle) brings light together, like a magnifying glass.
questions: Why does a pencil look bent in water?
Light bends as it leaves water and enters air.
Light's speed changes in different materials
When light goes from air into glass, it bends:
Entering a denser medium, light slows and bends towards the normal.
Why does a pond look shallower than it is?
Bending of light makes the bottom appear raised.
The refractive index of glass is about:
Glass has a refractive index around 1.5.
In which material does light travel fastest?
Light is fastest in air or vacuum.
A convex lens is thicker in the middle and makes things look bigger.
What safety lesson does refraction teach?
Water may be deeper than it looks
Never assume water is shallow just by looking.
